title: Given n nodes labeled 0 to n minus 1 and a list of undirected edges, determine whether these edges form a valid tree, meaning the graph is fully connected and contains no cycle.
shortTitle: Graph Valid Tree — connected and no cycle

s1_definition.profdef: A graph is a valid tree if and only if it has exactly n minus one edges and is connected, which together forbid cycles. The check verifies the edge count then confirms connectivity with a single traversal from any node reaching all n nodes, or equivalently uses Union-Find to detect any cycle while unioning edges.
s1_definition.analogy: Think of verifying that an organizational reporting structure is a clean tree: everyone is reachable from the top and there are no circular reporting loops. With n people, a valid tree has exactly n minus one reporting links, and starting from anyone you can reach everyone. Too many links means a loop, too few means someone is disconnected.
s1_definition.oneliner: Valid tree iff exactly n minus one edges and fully connected; verify with a single traversal reaching all nodes or with Union-Find detecting no cycle.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** A graph is a valid tree if and only if it has exactly n minus one edges and is connected, which together forbid cycles. The check verifies the edge count then confirms connectivity with a single traversal from any node reaching all n nodes, or equivalently uses Union-Find to detect any cycle while unioning edges.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Think of verifying that an organizational reporting structure is a clean tree: everyone is reachable from the top and there are no circular reporting loops. With n people, a valid tree has exactly n minus one reporting links, and starting from anyone you can reach everyone. Too many links means a loop, too few means someone is disconnected.

**One line to remember:** Valid tree iff exactly n minus one edges and fully connected; verify with a single traversal reaching all nodes or with Union-Find detecting no cycle.

sections.s2_technical:
First check the edge count: a tree on n nodes has precisely n minus one edges. If the count differs, it cannot be a tree, so return false immediately. For example: `if (edges.length != n - 1) return false;`.

Given exactly n minus one edges, the graph is a tree if and only if it is connected, because n minus one edges with full connectivity cannot contain a cycle. Build an adjacency list and run a BFS or DFS from node zero, counting reachable nodes. For example: `visited.add(0); traverse; return visitedCount == n;`.

Alternatively, Union-Find processes each edge by unioning its endpoints; if an edge connects two nodes already in the same set, that edge closes a cycle and the graph is not a tree. For example: `if (find(u) == find(v)) return false; else union(u, v);`, and after all edges the number of components must be one.

Both run in near-linear time, the traversal in nodes plus edges and Union-Find in edges times the inverse Ackermann factor. A senior nuance is that the edge-count check plus connectivity is sufficient precisely because of the tree identity, so I do not need to separately test for cycles once both hold, and Union-Find elegantly fuses the cycle check and connectivity into one pass.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — At National Bank of India, an approval-hierarchy configuration must form a valid tree: every unit reachable from the root with no circular approval loops. The system must validate this. This is exactly how Graph Valid Tree works — connected and acyclic.

Problem 2 — A bad configuration could disconnect a unit or create an approval loop, both of which must be rejected. This is exactly why the edge-count plus connectivity check is used.

The mini-project builds an `ApprovalTreeValidator` using edge count plus BFS connectivity, a `BankLogFormatter`, and a runnable demo.

sections.s5_journey:
The first input has five units and four edges connecting zero to one, two, three, and one to four.

Step 1: The edge count is four, which equals five minus one, so the count check passes.

Step 2: BFS starts at unit zero, visiting it and enqueuing its neighbors one, two, and three.

Step 3: Processing those, unit one enqueues unit four, and the search eventually visits all five units.

Step 4: The reachable count is five, equal to n, so the graph is connected and, with the right edge count, is a valid tree, returning true.

Step 5: The second input has four units and three edges forming a cycle among one, two, three while unit zero has no edge. The edge count is three which equals four minus one, so the count check passes but is misleading here.

Step 6: BFS from unit zero visits only unit zero, since it has no neighbors, giving a reachable count of one which is less than four, so the graph is disconnected and not a valid tree, returning false.

sections.s5b_flow:
```text
  valid: n=5, edges 0-1,0-2,0-3,1-4 (4 == n-1)
         BFS from 0 reaches {0,1,2,3,4}=5 → connected → TREE

  invalid: n=4, edges 1-2,2-3,3-1 (3 == n-1 but...)
         node 0 isolated; 1-2-3 form a cycle
         BFS from 0 reaches {0}=1 < 4 → disconnected → NOT a tree

  rule: edges==n-1 AND connected ⇔ valid tree (then no cycle guaranteed)
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Graph Valid Tree asks whether a set of undirected edges on n nodes forms a tree, which means the graph is connected and has no cycle. The clean characterization I rely on is that a graph is a tree if and only if it has exactly n minus one edges and is connected. Those two conditions together automatically forbid a cycle, so I never need a separate cycle test once both hold.

I first check the edge count, returning false immediately if it is not n minus one. Given the right count, I build an adjacency list and run a single BFS or DFS from any node, counting how many nodes I reach. If I reach all n, the graph is connected and therefore a valid tree; if I reach fewer, it is disconnected and invalid. The Union-Find alternative processes each edge by unioning its endpoints, declaring failure if an edge joins two nodes already in the same component, which is a cycle, and finally requiring a single component.

The reasoning interviewers want is why the edge-count-plus-connectivity test is sufficient: with exactly n minus one edges, connectivity leaves no room for a cycle, so the two checks replace an explicit cycle search. Both approaches are near-linear.

In my project at National Bank of India, an approval-hierarchy configuration had to form a valid tree so every unit was reachable from the root with no circular approval loops. I validated it by confirming the edge count was n minus one and that a single traversal reached every unit, which rejected configurations that either disconnected a unit or introduced an approval cycle.
